replacement: The Christian nations of our age seem to me to present a most alarming spectacle. The movement carrying them along is so strong that it cannot be stopped, but it is not yet so fast that it cannot be guided. Their fate is in their own hands, though in a little while it may no longer be. The first duty of those who direct our affairs at this time is to educate the democracy: to warm its faith, if that is possible; to purify its morals; to direct its energies; to replace its inexperience with a knowledge of practical affairs, and its blind impulses with an understanding of its true interests; to adapt its government to time and place; and to change it to suit the events and the people of the age. A new science of politics is needed for a new world. Yet this is what we think about least. Launched into the middle of a rapid stream, we stubbornly fix our eyes on the ruins still visible on the shore we have left, while the current sweeps us along and drives us backward toward the abyss.

The result has been that the democratic revolution has taken place only in the material parts of society, without the accompanying change in laws, ideas, customs, and mores that was needed to make such a revolution beneficial. We have gotten a democracy, but without the conditions that would reduce its vices and bring out its natural advantages. And although we already see the evils it brings, we do not know the benefits it may offer.

While the power of the Crown, supported by the aristocracy, governed the nations of Europe in peace, society had, amid its misery, several advantages that are now hard to appreciate or even imagine. The power of one part of his subjects was an insurmountable barrier to the prince’s tyranny. The monarch felt that the multitude saw him as almost divine, and the respect he inspired gave him a reason to use his power justly. However high they stood above the people, the nobles could not help taking the calm and kindly interest in its fate that a shepherd takes in his flock. Without acknowledging the poor as their equals, they watched over the destiny of those whose welfare Providence had entrusted to their care. The people had never conceived of a social condition different from their own, and they did not expect ever to rank with their chiefs. They accepted benefits from their superiors without questioning their rights. They grew attached to them when they were merciful and just, and they submitted to their exactions without resistance or servility, as to the unavoidable visitations of the arm of God. Custom and the habits of the time had also created a kind of law amid the violence and set certain limits to oppression. The noble never suspected that anyone would try to deprive him of the privileges he believed to be legitimate, and the serf regarded his own inferiority as a consequence of the unchangeable order of nature. It is therefore easy to imagine that a mutual exchange of goodwill took place between two classes so differently endowed by fate. Inequality and misery existed in society then, but the souls of neither class were degraded. Men are not corrupted by exercising power or debased by the habit of obeying. They are corrupted by exercising a power they believe to be illegitimate, and by obeying a rule they consider usurped and oppressive. On one side were wealth, strength, and leisure, along with the refinements of luxury, the elegance of taste, the pleasures of wit, and the religion of art. On the other were labor and a crude ignorance. Yet among this coarse and ignorant multitude it was not uncommon to find energetic passions, generous feelings, deep religious convictions, and independent virtues. A body politic organized in this way could boast of its stability, its power, and above all its glory.

But the scene has now changed. Gradually the two ranks are mingling. The divisions that once separated mankind are being lowered, property is being divided, power is shared, the light of intelligence is spreading, and the abilities of all classes are being cultivated equally. The state becomes democratic, and the empire of democracy is slowly and peacefully introduced into the institutions and customs of the nation. I can imagine a society in which all men would profess an equal attachment and respect for the laws, of which they are the common authors. The authority of the state would be respected as necessary, though not as divine, and the subject’s loyalty to the chief magistrate would be not a passion but a calm and rational conviction. Every individual would possess rights he is sure to keep, and a kind of manly confidence and mutual courtesy would arise among all classes, equally far from pride and from baseness. The people, well aware of their true interests, would accept that to enjoy the advantages of society they must meet its demands. In such a state of things, the voluntary association of citizens could take the place of the individual efforts of the nobles, and the community would be protected equally from anarchy and from oppression.

There is one country in the world where the great revolution I am speaking of seems to have nearly reached its natural limits. It has been carried out there with ease and simplicity. Or rather, that country has arrived at the consequences of the democratic revolution we are going through without having experienced the revolution itself. The emigrants who settled on the shores of America at the beginning of the seventeenth century separated the democratic principle from all the principles that held it back in the old communities of Europe, and they transplanted it, unmixed, to the New World. There it has been allowed to grow in perfect freedom and to bring out its consequences in the laws by shaping the customs of the country.

It seems to me beyond doubt that sooner or later we will arrive, like the Americans, at an almost complete equality of conditions. But I do not conclude from this that we will necessarily be led to draw the same political consequences that the Americans have drawn from a similar social organization. I am far from supposing that they have chosen the only form of government a democracy can adopt. But the fact that the same underlying cause shapes laws and customs in both countries is enough to explain why we have such an immense interest in knowing its effects in each of them.

Whenever a point could be established from written documents, I went to the original text and to the most authentic and respected works. I have cited my authorities in the notes, and anyone may consult them. Whenever the question concerned an opinion, a political custom, or a remark about the customs of the country, I tried to consult the best-informed men I met. If the point was important or doubtful, I was not satisfied with one witness, but formed my opinion from the testimony of several. Here the reader must necessarily take my word. I could often have named people he knows, or who deserve to be known, as proof of what I say, but I have carefully avoided doing so. A stranger often hears important truths at his host’s fireside that the host would perhaps hide from the ear of a friend. The host consoles himself with his guest for the silence he is otherwise bound to keep, and the shortness of the traveler’s stay removes any fear that he will be indiscreet. I carefully noted down every conversation of this kind as soon as it happened, but these notes will never leave my writing case. I would rather weaken the force of my statements than add my name to the list of strangers who repay generous hospitality with later vexation and annoyance.

Many people in Europe tend to believe without saying so, or to say without believing, that one of the great advantages of universal suffrage is that it puts the direction of public affairs in the hands of men who deserve the public’s confidence. They admit that the people cannot govern itself, but they assert that it is always sincerely disposed to promote the welfare of the state, and that it instinctively picks out those who share its good intentions and are best fit to hold supreme authority. I confess that what I observed in America does not agree with these opinions at all. When I arrived in the United States I was surprised to find so much distinguished talent among the governed and so little among the heads of the government. It is a well-established fact that today the ablest men in the United States are very rarely placed at the head of affairs, and it must be acknowledged that this has come about as democracy has overstepped all its former limits. The breed of American statesmen has clearly declined remarkably over the last fifty years.

g [ The comfortable circumstances of secondary officials in the United States also result from another cause, which is independent of the general tendencies of democracy. Every kind of private business is very lucrative, and the state would not be served at all if it did not pay its servants. The country is in the position of a commercial enterprise that is obliged to sustain costly competition, in spite of its taste for economy.]

Another cause tends to make the efforts of a democratic government less persevering than those of an aristocracy. The lower classes are not only less alert than the higher orders to the good or bad chances of the future, but they also suffer far more keenly from present privations. The nobleman does risk his life, but the chance of glory is as great as the chance of harm. If he gives up a large part of his income to the state, he deprives himself for a time of the pleasures of wealth. But for the poor man, death is adorned with no pomp or renown, and the taxes that are irksome to the rich are fatal to him.

Nothing is more embarrassing in the ordinary course of life than this irritable patriotism of the Americans. A stranger may be quite willing to praise many of the institutions of their country, but he asks permission to criticize some of the peculiarities he observes, and that permission is firmly refused. America is therefore a free country in which, lest anyone be hurt by your remarks, you are not allowed to speak freely of private individuals or of the state, of the citizens or of the authorities, of public or of private undertakings, or in short of anything at all, except the climate and the soil. And even then Americans will be found ready to defend one or the other, as if the inhabitants of the country had designed them.

Effects of the tyranny of the majority have so far been felt more in customs than in the conduct of society — They check the development of leading characters — Democratic republics organized like the United States put the practice of courting favor within the reach of the many — Proofs of this spirit in the United States — Why there is more patriotism in the people than in those who govern in its name.

Accidental or Providential Causes Which Contribute to the Maintenance of the Democratic Republic in the United States The Union has no neighbors — No metropolis — The Americans have had the chances of birth in their favor — America an empty country — How this circumstance contributes powerfully to the maintenance of the democratic republic in America — How the American wilds are peopled — Avidity of the Anglo-Americans in taking possession of the solitudes of the New World — Influence of physical prosperity upon the political opinions of the Americans.

I could easily list a great number of secondary causes that have helped establish the democratic republic of the United States and that help maintain it. But among these favorable elements I discern two principal ones, which I hasten to point out. I have already observed that the origin of the American settlements can be seen as the first and most effective cause to which the present prosperity of the United States may be attributed. The Americans had the chances of birth in their favor. Their forefathers brought with them into the country that equality of conditions from which the democratic republic has very naturally grown. Nor was this all they did. Besides this republican state of society, the early settlers handed down to their descendants the customs, mores, and opinions that contribute most to the success of a republican form of government. When I reflect on the consequences of this first circumstance, I seem to see the destiny of America contained in the first Puritan who landed on those shores, just as the whole human race was represented by the first man.

Others have so often described the favorable influence of America’s material prosperity on the institutions of that country, and I myself have so often mentioned it, that I shall not dwell on it beyond adding a few facts. People commonly hold a mistaken notion that the deserts of America are peopled by European emigrants who land every year on the coasts of the New World, while the American population grows and multiplies on the soil its forefathers tilled. In fact, the European settler usually arrives in the United States without friends, and sometimes without resources. To survive he has to work for hire, and he rarely goes beyond the belt of industrious population next to the ocean. The desert cannot be explored without capital or credit, and the body must be accustomed to the hardships of a new climate before it can be exposed to the risks of forest life. It is the Americans themselves who leave the places of their birth every day to acquire extensive lands in a remote country. Thus the European leaves his cottage for the shores across the Atlantic, and the American, who was born on that very coast, plunges in his turn into the wilds of Central America. This double emigration never stops. It begins in the remotest parts of Europe, it crosses the Atlantic Ocean, and it advances across the solitudes of the New World. Millions of men are marching at once toward the same horizon. Their language, their religion, and their customs differ, but their object is the same. The gifts of fortune are promised in the West, and to the West they turn their steps. *b

In France, simple tastes, orderly habits, domestic affections, and the attachment men feel to the place of their birth are regarded as great guarantees of the peace and happiness of the State. But in America nothing seems more harmful to society than these virtues. The French Canadians have faithfully preserved the traditions of their original customs, and they are already short of room on their small territory. This little community, which has only recently begun to exist, will soon fall prey to the calamities that afflict old nations. In Canada the most educated, patriotic, and humane inhabitants make extraordinary efforts to make the people dissatisfied with the simple enjoyments that still content them. There, the seductions of wealth are praised with as much zeal as the charms of an honest but limited income are praised in the Old World. More effort is spent there on exciting the passions of the citizens than elsewhere on calming them. If we listen to their praises, we shall hear that nothing is more admirable than to trade the pure and homely pleasures that even the poor man enjoys in his own country for the dull delights of prosperity under a foreign sky. We shall hear that it is admirable to leave the family hearth and the turf beneath which one’s forefathers sleep, in short, to abandon the living and the dead in search of fortune.

In New England I met men who were about to leave a country where they could have lived comfortably, to seek their fortune in the wilds. Not far from there, in Canada, I found a French population crowded into a narrow strip of land even though the same wilds lay close by. The emigrant from the United States bought a large estate with what he earned in a short period of work, while the Canadian paid as much for land as he would have paid in France. Nature offers the solitudes of the New World to Europeans, but they do not always know how to turn her gifts to account. Other peoples of America have the same physical conditions for prosperity as the Anglo-Americans, but without their laws and their customs, and these peoples are wretched. The laws and customs of the Anglo-Americans are therefore the effective cause of their greatness, which is the object of my inquiry.

I am far from supposing that the American laws are excellent in themselves. I do not think they apply to all democratic peoples, and several of them seem dangerous to me, even in the United States. Still, no one can deny that American legislation, taken as a whole, suits the genius of its people and the nature of its country extremely well. The American laws are therefore good, and a large share of the success of democratic government in America must be credited to them. But I do not believe they are the main cause of that success. They seem to me to have more influence on the social happiness of the Americans than the nature of the country does. Yet there is reason to believe that their effect is still smaller than that of the customs of the people.

I am no longer comparing the Anglo-American States with foreign nations. I am contrasting them with each other and trying to discover why they are so unlike. The arguments drawn from the nature of the country and from differences in legislation are all set aside here. Some other cause must be found, and what other cause can there be except the customs of the people?

The Anglo-Americans, if transported into Europe, would be obliged to modify their laws — A distinction must be made between democratic institutions and American institutions — Democratic laws may be conceived that are better than, or at least different from, those the American democracy has adopted — The example of America only proves that it is possible to regulate democracy with the help of customs and legislation.

I have asserted that the success of democratic institutions in the United States depends more on the laws themselves and the customs of the people than on the nature of the country. But does it follow that the same causes would produce the same results if they were put to work elsewhere? And if the country is no adequate substitute for laws and customs, can laws and customs in their turn substitute for the country? We can easily see that we lack what we would need to answer this question. There are other peoples in the New World besides the Anglo-Americans, and since the same physical circumstances affect them, they can fairly be compared with the Anglo-Americans. But no nations outside America have adopted the same laws and customs while lacking the physical advantages that belong to the Anglo-Americans. So there is no standard of comparison, and we can only venture an opinion on this subject.

It is easy to see why I undertook the inquiries above. The question discussed here interests not only the United States but the whole world. It concerns not one nation but all mankind. If nations whose social condition is democratic could remain free only while they lived in the wilds, we could only despair of the future of the human race. For democracy is rapidly extending its sway, and the wilds are gradually filling with people. If it were true that laws and customs are not enough to maintain democratic institutions, what refuge would remain open to nations except the despotism of a single individual? I know that there are many worthy people today who are not alarmed by this alternative, and who are so tired of liberty that they would be glad of rest, far from the storms that accompany it. But these people do not know well the harbor toward which they are headed. Their memories deceive them so much that they judge the tendency of absolute power by what it was in the past, and not by what it might become today.

If absolute power were re-established among the democratic nations of Europe, I am persuaded that it would take a new form and appear with features unknown to our forefathers. There was a time in Europe when the laws and the consent of the people had given princes almost unlimited authority, but they hardly ever made use of it. I am not speaking of the prerogatives of the nobility, of the authority of the supreme courts of justice, of corporations and their chartered rights, or of provincial privileges. These softened the blows of the sovereign authority and kept a spirit of resistance alive in the nation. Apart from these political institutions, which kept the love of freedom alive in the public mind, however opposed they may have been to personal liberty, and which may be considered useful in that respect, the customs and opinions of the nation confined royal authority within barriers that were no less powerful for being less conspicuous. Religion, the affections of the people, the kindness of the prince, the sense of honor, family pride, provincial prejudices, custom, and public opinion all limited the power of kings and held their authority within an invisible circle. The constitution of nations was despotic at that time, but their customs were free. Princes had the right, but they had neither the means nor the desire, to do whatever they pleased.

As long as family feeling was alive, the man who opposed oppression was never alone. He looked around him and found his clients, his hereditary friends, and his relatives. If this support was lacking, his ancestors sustained him and his descendants inspired him. But when inherited estates are divided, and a few years are enough to blur the distinctions of a race, where can family feeling be found? What force can there be in the customs of a country that has changed and is still constantly changing its face? In such a country every act of tyranny has a precedent and every crime an example. Nothing is so old that its age can save it from destruction, and nothing so unheard of that its novelty can prevent it from being done. What resistance can customs offer when they are so pliant that they have already often given way? What strength can even public opinion have kept, when no twenty persons are connected by a common tie? When not a single man, family, chartered corporation, class, or free institution has the power to represent or assert that opinion? When every citizen, equally weak, equally poor, and equally dependent, has only his personal helplessness to set against the organized force of the government?

The annals of France offer nothing like the condition into which that country might then be thrown. It is better compared to the times of old, to those hideous eras of Roman oppression, when the customs of the people were corrupted, their traditions wiped out, their habits destroyed, and their opinions shaken. Freedom, driven out of the laws, could find no refuge in the land. Nothing protected the citizens, and the citizens no longer protected themselves. Human nature was the plaything of man, and princes wore out the mercy of Heaven before they exhausted the patience of their subjects. Those who hope to revive the monarchy of Henry IV or of Louis XIV seem to me to be afflicted with mental blindness. When I consider the present condition of several European nations, a condition toward which all the others are tending, I am led to believe that they will soon be left with no other alternative than democratic liberty or the tyranny of the Caesars. *n

And indeed it deserves consideration whether men are to be entirely emancipated or entirely enslaved, whether their rights are to be made equal or wholly taken away from them. Suppose the rulers of society were reduced either to raising the crowd gradually to their own level or to pushing the citizens below the level of humanity. Would not the doubts of many be resolved, the consciences of many be healed, and the community be prepared to make great sacrifices with little difficulty? In that case, the gradual growth of democratic customs and institutions should be regarded not as the best means of preserving freedom but as the only one. Even without liking democratic government, one might adopt it as the most workable and the fairest remedy for the present ills of society.

Anyone who, after reading this book, imagines that I wrote it to hold up the laws and customs of the Anglo-Americans as a model for all democratic peoples would be making a very great mistake. Such a reader must have paid more attention to the form of my ideas than to their substance. My aim has been to show, by the example of America, that there may be laws, and especially customs, that allow a democratic people to remain free. But I am very far from thinking that we should follow the example of the American democracy and copy the means it has used to reach its ends. I am well aware of the influence that the nature of a country and its political precedents have on a constitution, and I would regard it as a great misfortune for mankind if liberty were to exist all over the world in the same forms.

This, then, is the subject on which it is most important for each of us to hold fixed ideas. Unhappily, it is also the subject on which it is hardest for each of us, left alone, to settle our opinions by the force of reason alone. Only minds unusually free from the ordinary anxieties of life, minds that are at once penetrating, subtle, and trained in thinking, can sound the depths of these most necessary truths, even with the help of much time and care. Indeed, we see that these philosophers are themselves almost always wrapped in uncertainties. At every step the natural light that illuminates their path grows dimmer and less secure. In spite of all their efforts, they have so far discovered only a small number of conflicting ideas, on which the human mind has been tossed about for thousands of years without getting a firmer grip on the truth or even finding anything new in its errors. Studies of this kind are far above the average capacity of people. And even if most of mankind were capable of such pursuits, it is clear that they would still lack the leisure to pursue them. Fixed ideas of God and of human nature are indispensable to the daily conduct of people’s lives, but the conduct of their lives prevents them from acquiring such ideas.

As castes disappear and the classes of society draw closer together, as mores, customs, and laws change through the tumultuous contact of people with one another, as new facts arise, as new truths come to light, as ancient opinions fade and others take their place, the image of an ideal perfection, always on the wing, presents itself to the human mind. Continual changes then occur at every moment under everyone’s eyes. The position of some is made worse, and he learns only too well that no people and no individual, however enlightened, can claim to be infallible. The condition of others is improved, and from this he infers that man is endowed with an indefinite capacity for improvement. His setbacks teach him that no one may hope to have found absolute good; his successes spur him to pursue it without end. Thus, always seeking, always falling to rise again, often disappointed but not discouraged, he moves unceasingly toward that immeasurable greatness, so dimly visible at the end of the long road that humanity has yet to travel. It is hard to believe how many facts flow naturally from the philosophical theory of the indefinite perfectibility of man, or how strong an influence it has even on people who live entirely for action and not for thought, and who seem to conform their actions to it without knowing anything about it. I stop an American sailor and ask why the ships of his country are built to last such a short time. He answers without hesitation that the art of navigation is making such rapid progress every day that the finest vessel would become almost useless if it lasted beyond a certain number of years. In these words, which fell by chance and on a particular subject from a man of rough education, I recognize the general and systematic idea on which a great people directs all its affairs.

When the heroes and customs of antiquity are often brought onto the stage, and playwrights faithfully follow the rules of old precedent, that is enough to conclude that the democratic classes have not yet gained the upper hand in the theaters. In the preface to “Britannicus,” Racine very humbly apologizes for having placed Junia among the Vestals, who, according to Aulus Gellius, he says, “admitted no one below six years of age nor above ten.” We may be sure he would neither have accused himself of this offense nor defended himself against criticism if he had been writing for our contemporaries. A fact of this kind shows the state of literature at the time, and it shows the state of society itself as well. A democratic stage does not prove that the nation is in a state of democracy, because, as we have just seen, even in aristocracies democratic tastes may influence the drama. But when the spirit of aristocracy reigns exclusively on the stage, that fact proves beyond refutation that the whole of society is aristocratic. One may boldly infer that the same lettered and learned class that sways the playwrights also commands the people and governs the country.

The refined tastes and arrogant bearing of an aristocracy will rarely fail to lead it, when it controls the stage, to make a kind of selection within human nature. Some conditions of society hold its chief interest, and the scenes that depict their customs are preferred on the stage. Certain virtues, and even certain vices, are thought to deserve a place there more than others, and these are applauded while all the rest are shut out. On the stage as elsewhere, an aristocratic audience wants to meet only people of quality and to share the emotions of kings. The same goes for style: an aristocracy tends to impose on playwrights certain modes of expression that set the key in which everything must be delivered. In this way the stage often comes to depict only one side of man, or sometimes even to represent what cannot be found in human nature at all, rising above nature and going beyond it.

When the world was managed by a few rich and powerful individuals, these people liked to hold a lofty idea of the duties of man. They were fond of declaring that it is praiseworthy to forget oneself, and that good should be done without hope of reward, as God himself does it. Such were the standard moral opinions of that time. I doubt whether men were more virtuous in aristocratic ages than in others. But they talked ceaselessly about the beauty of virtue, and they studied its usefulness only in private. But now that the imagination takes less lofty flights and every man’s thoughts are centered on himself, moralists are alarmed by this idea of self-sacrifice, and they no longer dare to offer it to the human mind. They therefore content themselves with asking whether the personal advantage of each member of the community does not lie in working for the good of all. When they hit on some point where private interest and public interest meet and merge, they are eager to bring it to notice. Observations of this kind gradually multiply. What was only a single remark becomes a general principle, and it is held to be true that man serves himself in serving his fellow creatures, and that his private interest is to do good.

The Americans advance enormously in productive industry because every one of them throws himself into it at the same time. For that very reason they face very unexpected and formidable troubles. Everyone is in commerce, so their commercial affairs depend on causes too varied and tangled for anyone to predict what trouble may come. Everyone is more or less in productive industry, so at the slightest jolt to business every private fortune is endangered at once, and the state itself is shaken. I believe that these recurring commercial panics are a disease native to the democratic nations of our age. It can be made less dangerous, but it cannot be cured, since it springs not from accidents but from the temperament of these nations.

This applies exactly to the subject we are now considering. In an aristocratic community, all men are fixed irrevocably in their places by profession, property, and birth. The members of each class regard themselves as children of one family and feel a constant, lively sympathy for one another, which the citizens of a democracy can never feel to the same degree. But the several classes do not feel the same way toward one another. Among an aristocratic people, each caste has its own opinions, feelings, rights, customs, and ways of living. So the men of each caste do not resemble the mass of their fellow citizens. They do not think or feel in the same way, and they hardly believe that they belong to the same human race. They therefore cannot fully understand what others feel, or judge others by themselves. Yet they are sometimes eager to help one another, and this does not contradict my earlier remark. These aristocratic institutions made beings of one and the same race very different, but they nevertheless tied them to one another by close political bonds. The serf had no natural interest in the fate of nobles, yet he still thought himself obliged to devote his person to the service of whichever noble happened to be his lord. And although the noble considered himself of a different nature from his serfs, he nevertheless held that his duty and his honor required him to defend, at the risk of his own life, those who lived on his lands.

In no country has such constant care been taken as in America to draw two clearly separate lines of action for the two sexes and to have them keep pace with each other, but on paths that are always different. American women never manage the family’s outside affairs, or run a business, or take part in political life. Nor, on the other hand, are they ever forced to do the rough labor of the fields or any of those heavy tasks that demand physical strength. No family is so poor as to be an exception to this rule. If an American woman cannot escape the quiet circle of domestic occupations, neither is she ever forced to go beyond it. So it is that the women of America, who often show a masculine strength of understanding and a manly energy, generally keep great delicacy of personal appearance and always keep the habits of women, although they sometimes prove that they have the hearts and minds of men.

One might suppose that the final consequence and necessary effect of democratic institutions is to throw all members of the community together in private as well as public life, and to force them all to live in common. But that would be to give the equality that arises from democracy a very crude and oppressive form. No state of society and no laws can make men so alike that education, fortune, and tastes will not put some differences between them. And although different men may sometimes find it in their interest to combine for the same purposes, they will never make it their pleasure. They will therefore always tend to evade the provisions of the law, whatever those may be. Departing in some one respect from the circle within which they were meant to be confined, they will set up, close beside the great political community, small private circles united by the similarity of their conditions, habits, and customs.

In aristocracies men are separated from one another by lofty, fixed barriers; in democracies they are divided by a multitude of small, almost invisible threads, which are constantly broken or moved from place to place. Thus, whatever the progress of equality, a great number of small private communities will always form within the general bounds of political society in democratic nations. But none of them will resemble in its customs the highest class in aristocracies.

When public employments are few, poorly paid, and insecure, while the various lines of business are numerous and profitable, the new and eager desires that the principle of equality produces turn from every side toward business, not toward official duties. But if, while the ranks of society are growing more equal, the education of the people stays incomplete, or their spirit is anything but bold, and if commerce and industry, held back in their growth, offer only slow and difficult ways of making a fortune, then the members of the community, despairing of improving their own condition, rush to the head of the state and demand its help. To relieve their own needs at the expense of the public treasury seems to them the easiest and most open way, if not the only one, to rise above a condition that no longer satisfies them. Place-hunting becomes the most widely followed of all trades. This must be especially so in those great centralized monarchies where paid offices are immensely numerous and the tenure of them fairly secure, so that no one despairs of getting a place and enjoying it as undisturbedly as an inherited fortune.

Look closely at our contemporaries and dig down to the roots of their political opinions, and you will meet some of the ideas I have just described. The agreement may perhaps come as a surprise, among men who so often disagree. Americans hold that in every State the supreme power ought to come from the people. Once that power exists, however, they can imagine hardly any limit to it, and they are ready to concede that it has the right to do whatever it likes. They have not the faintest notion of special privileges for cities, families or persons. It seems never to have occurred to them that the same laws might fail to be applied, with strict uniformity, to every part and every inhabitant. These same opinions are spreading further in Europe. They are even working their way into the nations that most vehemently reject the sovereignty of the people. Those nations trace the supreme power to a different source but attribute the same characteristics to it. In all of them the idea of intermediate powers is growing faint and being erased. The idea of rights belonging inherently to certain individuals is fast vanishing from men’s minds, and the idea that society at large is omnipotent and sole authority is rising to fill the space. As social conditions grow more equal and men more alike, these ideas take root and spread. Equality produces them, and they in turn speed equality along.
